title: Client fragmentation and proxy-hop cost profiles
summary: Field notes + microbenchmarks exploring how client-side write patterns, TLS record sizes, and proxy hop buffering interact to produce tail-latency volatility. Includes experimental methodology, representative numbers, and next-step mitigations for production SLOs.
content:
Purpose and motivation:

We observed a handful of customer incidents where seemingly identical requests had 2–6x tail latency variance when routed through the edge proxy vs. direct-to-runtime. Initial hypothesis centered on backend queueing; deeper profiling shows client-side fragmentation (small writes), TLS record boundary effects, and per-hop buffering/resend behavior are the dominant contributors in our reproduced workload. This doc captures the test harness, measured signals, short explanations for root causes, and practical mitigations to evaluate in Dedicated/Hosted deployments.

High level results (executive TL;DR):
- Small client writes (sub-1KB) + Nagle-enabled TCP on some clients -> extra 0.5–12 ms per request on median depending on RTT and proxy behavior.
- TLS record aggregation matters: 16KB vs 1KB record sizes shifted tail P99 by 10–30 ms in our lab (100ms RTT baseline).
- Per-proxy hop queuing and coalescing (envoy-like behavior) can amplify small-client write variance into multi-decade tail amplification when combined with uneven arrival patterns.
- Disabling Nagle on client SDKs and encouraging a single write path for initial prompt reduces P95/P99 noisiness without materially changing throughput.

Test harness and methodology:
- Environment: 3 AZ stub cluster (eu-west-1-like latency emulation). Test runner in colocated region and separate runner with introduced 100ms RTT via linux tc netem.
- Components instrumented: client SDK (Node/Python), edge proxy (Envoy v1.24 config used by infra), TCP/TLS kernel metrics (tcp_info, tcp_retransmits), runtime frontend (accept + dechunk), per-process eBPF traces for syscall timing.
- Workloads: synthetic text-gen prompt set with two modes: (A) single write of full prompt (mean size 6.1KB), (B) multi-write fragmentation to mimic streaming prompt assembly (3–8 writes, mean write size 512–1024B). Also streaming response mode (server-side chunking) to observe reverse direction effects.
- Runs: each experiment 1200 requests, 4 concurrent clients, warmup 200 requests. Capture full TTFB, wall-clock, kernel-level timings, and per-hop proxy queue length.

Representative numbers (100ms RTT injected):
- Mode A (single write, TLS record ~6KB): median latency 210 ms, P95 280 ms, P99 340 ms.
- Mode B (fragmented writes, TLS record boundaries at ~1KB): median latency 240 ms (+14%), P95 350 ms (+25%), P99 480 ms (+41%).
- Same as Mode B but with client TCP_NODELAY set (Nagle disabled): median 230 ms, P95 330 ms, P99 420 ms.
- Mode B + edge proxy config with aggressive write coalescing (100us flush delay): P99 spikes to 620 ms in worst runs correlated with brief bursts at ingress.
- Direct-to-runtime (no edge proxy) with Mode B: P99 390 ms, indicating proxy amplifies variability but majority of added cost comes from fragmentation + TLS boundary interactions.

Signals observed and root-cause hypotheses:
1) Small writes cause repeated system calls + smaller TLS records. Each TLS record adds framing and handshake overhead and prevents the kernel from amortizing congestion window growth efficiently at high RTTs.
2) Nagle interacts poorly with application-level flush patterns: some client SDKs do small writes and then linger, causing the kernel to delay transmission to coalesce, which increases latency in tail when combined with buffer pressure.
3) Proxy coalescing heuristics (Envoy flush timers and socket write buffering) intentionally wait a short window to batch writes. With steady traffic this is good, but with bursty/uneven arrival it increases jitter and couples per-connection delays into queued head-of-line delays inside proxy worker threads.
4) TLS record size alignment with TCP MSS matters: many small TLS records cause packetization inefficiency and more ACKs/retransmissions when loss occurs; we saw small increases in retransmit counts in Mode B.

Practical mitigations to explore (client + infra):
- Client SDK changes (high impact, low infra risk): enable TCP_NODELAY by default for server-initiated streaming flows or expose a per-request option; provide guidance for single-write prompt assembly; optional TLS record padding/coalescing in SDK before write.
- Edge proxy tuning (infra change): reduce coalescing flush timer for low-latency classes (e.g., 50us) or use adaptive flush that trades off latency variance vs. throughput based on per-route SLO tags. Also add per-connection histogram-based health metrics for flush-wait counts.
- Runtime frontend (defensive): accept and reframe small fragments using async gather before entering critical path; measure memory/cpu trade-off. Avoid synchronous syscalls per fragment in hot code path.
- SLO and routing policy: route latency-sensitive customers to a low-coalescing proxy fleet or Dedicated pools where we can enforce client-configured TCP/TLS knobs.

Short notes on measurement fidelity and limitations:
- Our lab uses tc netem to add uniform RTT; customer networks sometimes show asymmetric and multipath characteristics which can change absolute numbers.
- We only used Envoy v1.24 with typical config; other proxy implementations (varnish, nginx, cloud edge) may differ in flush heuristics.
- We did not model TLS record-level CPU cost for very small records on constrained CPUs — that's a separate axis for mobile clients.

Action items and next experiments (owner in parens):
- Roll a client-SDK opt-in flag (tcp_nodelay=true) and run A/B on internal staging to measure regression risk (Liam Wong).
- Create a small patch in runtime acceptor to batch small incoming fragments for 1ms before moving to main parser; measure CPU and memory overhead (Rahul Iyer).
- Prototype an adaptive proxy flush policy: route-level SLO tag -> flush-delay map, start with 50/250/1000us (Sofia Alvarez).
- Add telemetry: per-connection flush-waits, small-tls-record-count, application write syscalls per-request to our tracing and add to per-route dashboards (Maya Fernandez).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally focused on the network/payoff surface — not tokenization or model compute. The goal is to find high-leverage levers that reduce variance for latency-sensitive customers.
- If we push client-side defaults (tcp_nodelay), we should coordinate releases with SDK owners and include a compatibility note for platforms where disabling Nagle increases CPU/battery usage.

Appendix: quick commands used during profiling:
- netem setup (on client-router): tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 100ms loss 0.1%
- capture TLS records: sudo tshark -i eth0 -Y "ssl.record" -w records.pcap
- eBPF latency per-syscall: flamegraph-esque stack collector for write/sendfile (link to script in linked_artifacts).

Rough timeline recommendation:
- 2 weeks: SDK opt-in + telemetry additions (A/B test).
- 3–4 weeks: runtime batching POC + proxy adaptive flush prototype.
- 6–8 weeks: roll to a subset of Hosted clusters and measure customer-facing SLOs.

Open questions / discussion points:
- Are we comfortable trading slightly higher median latency for much lower P99 by changing proxy flush policy globally? (ops/strategy)
- Do we want to provide an explicit "low-latency" route that customers can opt into that has more expensive per-req CPU but lower flush delays?
- How will Dedicated customers want control surfaced — config flag vs support request?

-- End of notes --
